newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Yale school trains women for political office.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Yale school trains women for political office.

text.p: If there is a potential Margaret Thatcher somewhere in Kenya, the Ukraine -- or even the United States -- a unique programme at Yale University is designed to bring her out.

For the past four years, the Women's Campaign School has drawn dozens of aspiring women politicians from around the globe, teaching them how to overcome the barriers that have traditionally kept them from holding political office.
The intensive five-day course teaches everything from fund-raising to writing a catchy slogan to dealing with pesky reporters. The tuition fee is $750.

"Women have made great strides in the business world but what we haven't seen is more of an influx of women in politics," said Nancy Wyman, Connecticut's first woman comptroller and president of the Women's Campaign School.
"It's still a man's world in politics," Wyman, a Democrat, told Reuters. "Women really do start out at the bottom."
The school is geared to both candidates and campaign managers and classes are taught by seasoned politicians, campaign managers and consultants.

This year's session, which ended on June 8, drew 39 students from Canada, Haiti, Kenya, the Ukraine and the United States. A 40th student, from Japan, withdrew because of her advanced pregnancy. Among them were a former prime minister of Haiti, a sociologist from Ukraine and an aspiring candidate for city council in Scottsdale, Arizona.
TRAINING IN POLITICS
"We believe that women have to be trained in politics the same way they are trained in other fields," said Claudette Werleigh, who resigned as Haiti's prime minister in 1996.

She told Reuters she had not decided if she would make another bid for political office, but she said Haitian politics urgently needs more women. Men presently hold all 27 seats in the country's Senate and 84 of the 87 seats in the lower chamber, she said.

Astria Wong, a Hong Kong-born image consultant who lives in Scottsdale, Arizona, is gearing up to run for city council next year. When she contested in the previous election, she lost by just 1 percent of the popular vote, she said.
Her slogan? "Be Right, Vote Wong."

In the class on "Campaign Message and Slogan," Wong raised her hand and asked if it would be wise to keep using her old campaign leaflets and slogan in the next election since local issues had not changed all that much.
Perhaps she could, instructor Cathy Allen, a Seattle-based political consultant, said, but it would still be a good idea to conduct a new poll of voters' attitudes.

Wong said she faced a tough fight in Scottsdale, where only 2.3 percent of the population is Asian. "It's still a novelty for a Chinese American to run for office, especially a Chinese woman -- it's a no-no. But I'm a maverick," said the pro-environment and abortion rights Republican.

Allen, who has run more than 150 campaigns in 30 U.S. states and on three continents, emphasised the importance of sticking to a well-defined message -- a lesson many male politicians would do well to heed as well.

"Message is something that comes from the soul, is tested through the public, and delivered with passion, conviction and energy," she told her class. "You need the right, targeted message to go to the right, targeted people at the right time -- at least three to five times, in a variety of ways, through a variety of people."

But Allen said a political campaign should not be an attempt to educate the public; candidates should discern what is on the voters' minds and then pinpoint the part of their message that best taps into it.

Shirley Bean, a Bridgeport, Connecticut, city council member, was clearly charged up by the message. "I would like to run for U.S. Congress within the next four years," said Bean, an African American who works at People's Bank as a systems specialist in the residential lending department.
Consolata Ngondi, 31, flew for 14 hours from Kenya to attend the class. A human-rights lawyer in Nairobi, she is backing a presidential candidate in her country, Charity Ngilu, who shares her gender.

In Kenya, she said, "More and more women are realising that they're not going to get where they want to be by trying to change men's attitudes but by trying to get into decision-making positions themselves."

Only six of Kenya's 232 members of Parliament are women, said Ngondi, who hopes to run for Parliament eventually, perhaps in five years. "Women (in Africa) are going to bring back politics to focus on issues rather than individuals and images and ethnicity," she said.

"Women are more concerned with the issues because they have suffered the issues. They have suffered lack of proper education, they have suffered lack of health facilities, they have suffered the backlash from the economic reforms that are being made. And I think that those are the concerns that women are going to bring back to the centre stage of politics."
